title: Numbers and ages
rule: Numbers combine into larger numbers; in 21–99, say the ones before the tens. Age uses sein: Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt.

checkpoint.why: Age uses sein plus the cardinal number.

title: Family and possessives
rule: Mein, dein, sein and ihr show possession. Their endings depend on the noun’s gender and case.

checkpoint.why: Mutter is feminine nominative, so mein takes -e.

title: Food and ordering
rule: Use ich möchte for polite requests. In cafés, nouns usually function as direct objects.

checkpoint.why: Ich takes möchte.

title: Days, dates and time
rule: Days take am; clock times take um. The verb stays in second position.

checkpoint.why: Use am for days of the week.

title: Questions and answers
rule: W-questions begin with a question word, then the finite verb. Yes/no questions begin with the verb.

checkpoint.why: Woher asks about origin.

title: Negation: nicht and kein
rule: Use kein to negate indefinite nouns; nicht to negate verbs, adjectives, or specific parts of a sentence.

checkpoint.why: Hund is masculine accusative: keinen Hund.

title: Daily routines
rule: Describe habitual actions with present tense. Time can lead a sentence, with the finite verb second.

checkpoint.why: Ich requires trinke.

title: Places and directions
rule: Use nach with most cities/countries without articles; zu with people or destinations; in with locations.

checkpoint.why: Nach is used with cities as destinations.

title: Greetings and introductions
rule: Hallo is a greeting.

checkpoint.why: Hallo is a greeting.

title: Nouns and articles
rule: Tisch is masculine: der Tisch.

checkpoint.why: Tisch is masculine: der Tisch.

title: Present-tense verbs
rule: Wir takes the -en ending.

checkpoint.why: Wir takes the -en ending.

title: Basic word order
rule: In statements, the conjugated verb stays second.

checkpoint.why: In statements, the conjugated verb stays second.

title: Two-way prepositions
rule: In, an, auf and other two-way prepositions use accusative for direction and dative for location.
examples: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
The book lies on the table.

checkpoint.prompt: Ich lege das Buch auf ___ Tisch.
checkpoint.why: Direction onto a masculine noun uses accusative den.

title: Modal verbs
rule: Modal verbs change form with the subject and push the main infinitive to the end.

checkpoint.why: Wir takes müssen.

title: Comparatives and superlatives
rule: Use -er to compare; am ...-sten for adverbial superlatives. Some forms are irregular.

checkpoint.prompt: Dieses Auto ist ___ als das andere.
checkpoint.why: Comparative of schnell is schneller.

title: Reflexive verbs
rule: Reflexive pronouns refer back to the subject; their case depends on the verb.

checkpoint.why: Sich interessieren takes an accusative reflexive pronoun.

title: Imperatives and requests
rule: Commands use different forms for du, ihr and Sie. The polite imperative uses infinitive + Sie.

checkpoint.why: Formal Sie imperative uses infinitive + Sie.

title: Adjective endings
rule: Adjective endings depend on case, gender, and preceding article. After der in nominative masculine, use -e.

checkpoint.why: After der in nominative masculine, adjective ends -e.

title: Future plans
rule: Present tense with a future time word often expresses plans; werden + infinitive explicitly marks future.

checkpoint.why: Werden + infinitive forms future tense.

title: Travel and hotels
rule: Use polite requests and practical questions when checking in or traveling.

checkpoint.why: Perfekt uses habe + past participle reserviert.

title: Accusative articles
rule: Masculine der becomes den in accusative.

checkpoint.why: Masculine der becomes den in accusative.

title: Dative articles
rule: Helfen takes dative; die Frau becomes der Frau.

checkpoint.why: Helfen takes dative; die Frau becomes der Frau.

title: Perfect tense
rule: Kochen forms Perfekt with haben.

checkpoint.why: Kochen forms Perfekt with haben.

title: Separable verbs
rule: Aufstehen separates in a main clause.

checkpoint.why: Aufstehen separates in a main clause.

title: Genitive case
rule: Genitive shows relationships and possession; masculine and neuter articles use des and many nouns take -s/-es.

checkpoint.prompt: Wegen ___ Wetters bleiben wir zu Hause.
checkpoint.why: Wegen often takes genitive in formal German.

title: Infinitive with zu
rule: Infinitive clauses use zu; with separable verbs, zu goes between prefix and stem.
examples: Es ist wichtig, pünktlich zu sein.
It is important to be on time.

checkpoint.why: Infinitive construction uses zu + infinitive.

title: Past narratives: Präteritum
rule: Präteritum is common in writing and with sein, haben and modal verbs in speech.

checkpoint.why: War is Präteritum of sein.

title: Giving reasons and consequences
rule: Weil introduces a subordinate reason clause; deshalb introduces a main clause with inversion.
examples: Ich bin müde, weil ich arbeite.
I am tired because I work.
Es regnet, deshalb bleibe ich hier.
It rains, so I stay here.
Da es spät ist, gehen wir.
Since it is late, we leave.

checkpoint.prompt: Es regnet. Deshalb ___ ich zu Hause.
checkpoint.why: After deshalb in first position, the finite verb comes next.

title: Describing experiences
rule: Use Perfekt for events and descriptive phrases for reactions. Explain when and why things happened.

checkpoint.why: Gefallen forms Perfekt with hat + gefallen.

title: Conditional sentences
rule: Use wenn + verb-final clause for conditions. Konjunktiv II marks unreal or hypothetical conditions.
examples: Wenn ich Zeit habe, komme ich.
If I have time, I will come.
Wenn ich reich wäre, reiste ich.
If I were rich, I would travel.

checkpoint.prompt: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, ___ ich kommen.
checkpoint.why: Hypothetical conditional uses würde.

title: Opinions and discussion
rule: Support opinions with reasons and contrasting views; achten Sie auf the verb position after dass.

checkpoint.why: Dass sends the finite verb to the end.

title: Work and appointments
rule: Discuss scheduling, workplace requests, and obligations using polite structures.
examples: Ich bewerbe mich um eine Stelle.
I am applying for a job.
Ich bin für das Projekt zuständig.
I am responsible for the project.

checkpoint.why: Sich bewerben um + accusative is the fixed phrase.

title: Subordinate clauses
rule: After weil, the conjugated verb goes to the end.

checkpoint.prompt: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank ___.
checkpoint.why: After weil, the conjugated verb goes to the end.

title: Relative clauses
rule: The subject of the relative clause is nominative masculine: der.

checkpoint.prompt: Das ist der Mann, ___ hier arbeitet.
checkpoint.why: The subject of the relative clause is nominative masculine: der.

title: Konjunktiv II
rule: Hypothetical statements often use würde + infinitive.

checkpoint.prompt: Wenn ich mehr Zeit hätte, ___ ich reisen.
checkpoint.why: Hypothetical statements often use würde + infinitive.

title: Prepositions and cases
rule: Sich interessieren für takes accusative.

checkpoint.why: Sich interessieren für takes accusative.

title: Nominalization
rule: Nominalization turns verbs/adjectives into nouns, common in formal German. Infinitive nouns are neuter and capitalized.

checkpoint.why: Nominalized infinitives are neuter.

title: Participial adjectives
rule: Present participles describe ongoing action; past participles often describe results. Adjective endings still apply.

checkpoint.why: Past participle geschlossen describes a closed state; feminine definite adjective ends -e.

title: Passive with modal verbs
rule: Modal passive uses modal verb + past participle + werden; the modal verb is finite.

checkpoint.why: Passive with modal uses past participle + werden.

title: Advanced relative clauses
rule: Relative clauses may use prepositions and genitive pronouns. Prepositions determine the pronoun’s case.
examples: der Mann, mit dem ich spreche
das Thema, über das wir sprechen

checkpoint.prompt: Die Frau, mit ___ ich spreche, ist nett.
checkpoint.why: Mit requires dative; feminine relative pronoun is der.

title: Complex argumentation
rule: Use concessive and contrasting connectors to organize arguments. Mind verb placement.
examples: on the one hand … on the other

checkpoint.prompt: ___ die Kosten hoch sind, lohnt es sich.
checkpoint.why: Obwohl expresses concession, despite high costs.

title: Konjunktiv I and sources
rule: Use Konjunktiv I in formal reporting to distinguish a source’s claim from your own assertion.

checkpoint.prompt: Die Sprecherin sagt, die Lage ___ stabil.
checkpoint.why: Konjunktiv I of sein for third-person singular is sei.

title: Register and politeness
rule: Choose formal or informal register based on context; indirect questions are more polite and use verb-final order.

checkpoint.why: Indirect question uses verb-final clause.

title: Text cohesion and precision
rule: Use references, paraphrases and cohesive adverbs to avoid repetition and show relationships between claims.

checkpoint.prompt: Er hat wenig gelernt; ___ hat er bestanden.
checkpoint.why: Dennoch signals an unexpected result despite little study.

title: Passive voice
rule: Past passive uses wurde + past participle.

checkpoint.why: Past passive uses wurde + past participle.

title: Advanced connectors
rule: Obwohl introduces a concession: although.

checkpoint.why: Obwohl introduces a concession: although.

title: Reported speech
rule: Konjunktiv I (er habe) is used for reported speech.

checkpoint.why: Konjunktiv I (er habe) is used for reported speech.

title: Nuanced vocabulary
rule: Here allerdings emphasizes the statement: indeed.

checkpoint.prompt: Was bedeutet „allerdings“ hier: „Das ist allerdings schwierig“?
checkpoint.why: Here allerdings emphasizes the statement: indeed.
